Other names: Aith Waryaghar · Beni Ouriaghel · Sp.: 'Beni Urriaguel'
Region: Central Rif, around Ajdir and Alhucemas bay
Political position: The nucleus of Abd el-Krim's Rif Republic 1921–1926; the target of the 1925 Alhucemas landing and of chemical bombardment.
Notes: Abd el-Krim's own tribe. Hart's The Aith Waryaghar of the Moroccan Rif (1976) is the standard ethnography. Key research question: how a segmentary society with institutionalised feuding produced, within about two years, a centralised authority capable of suppressing the feud and fielding a coordinated army. That transformation — not the battles — is the real subject of the Rif war.

Other names: حزب الاستقلال · Hizb al-Istiqlal · Parti de l'Indépendance
Region: Fez, Rabat, Salé, Casablanca — urban and largely northern-urban in origin
Political position: Founded 1943–44; issued the Independence Manifesto of 11 January 1944; split in 1959 with the departure of the UNFP left.
Notes: Its urban, Arabophone, Fassi-notable social base is the fact most often left implicit — and it explains both its organisational strength and its distance from the rural resistance of the Middle and High Atlas and the Rif. The 1959 split producing the UNFP (Ben Barka, Bouabid, Ibrahim) is the founding division of post-independence Moroccan politics. Its rival in the French zone was Ouazzani's PDI; in the Spanish zone, Torres's Partido de Reformas Nacionales.

Region: High Atlas, Telouet and the Tizi n'Tichka pass
Political position: Backed Abdelhafid in 1907 and France from 1912; the central Moroccan instrument of the politique des grands caïds until 1955.
Notes: Power rested on control of the Tichka pass and the trade through it — salt, dates, minerals — then on French arms. Under the Protectorate the family held authority no pre-colonial caïd could have held, because the Makhzen counterweight had been removed. Property confiscated and the house broken politically after 1956.

Political position: A guich and makhzen-linked tribe of the Marrakech region; repeatedly involved in dynastic contests including the Hafidiya.
Notes: Stub. The guich tribes — holding land in return for military service — are an under-researched category in this workspace and they are the hinge between Makhzen fiscal-military organisation and tribal society. Others include the Oudaya, Cherarda and Bouakher. A dedicated study of the guich system is a priority.

Region: Western Rif and the hinterland of Tangier, Tetouan and Chefchaouen
Political position: Raisuni's base; a second and partly rival theatre of resistance in the Spanish zone, distinct from Abd el-Krim's Rif.
Notes: Arabic-speaking and religiously organised around sharifian lineages and zawiyas, in contrast to the Tarifit-speaking eastern Rif. The Jebala/Rif distinction is essential and is routinely collapsed in general accounts. Raisuni and Abd el-Krim were not allies; Rifian forces captured Raisuni in 1925.

Region: Atlantic plain around Casablanca and Settat
Political position: Site of the 30 July 1907 killings that triggered the French bombardment of Casablanca; subject of d'Amade's 1908 campaign.
Notes: The first region of Atlantic Morocco brought under sustained French military occupation, four years before the Protectorate. Its subsequent transformation into the agricultural and industrial hinterland of Casablanca makes it the best case study of colonial land expropriation and capitalist agriculture in Morocco — a subject this workspace has not begun.

Other names: Zaïans · Zaïanes · Zayanes (Sp.) · Izayyan · Aït Yaʿqoub and Aït Harkat (halves/sections)
Region: Central Middle Atlas, around Khénifra and the upper Oum er-Rbia
Political position: Makhzen-invested qaid under Hassan I; core of armed resistance to France 1914–1921; partial submission from June 1920.
Notes: French estimates give 4,000–4,200 tents under Mouha ou Hammou's authority — an estimate, not a census. The confederation assembled for specific occasions rather than operating as a standing hierarchy, which is why French strength figures swing so widely. Research gap: how decisions were taken in the Zaian jema'a. No Zaian-side written source has been used here.

Other names: Ait Atta · Aït 'Atta · Fr.: 'les Aït Atta'
Region: South-eastern High Atlas, Jbel Saghro, Dadès and Draa valleys, pre-Sahara
Political position: Among the last confederations brought under French control; held Bougafer in 1933 and ended it on negotiated terms.
Notes: Governed through a rotating, elected leadership system rather than hereditary chieftaincy — institutionalised constraint on any individual's power. French administrative categories, built around the caïd, handled this badly. One of the clearest cases where colonial vocabulary actively obscures Moroccan political reality. David M. Hart's ethnography is the standard reference and is itself a product of the colonial knowledge apparatus.
